title: How Unschooling Happens
author: Educating Hat Beasts
summary: A home-educating parent of an autistic son uses an extended pinball-repair anecdote to illustrate and formally define 'unschooling,' the child-led home-education approach that has no assigned textbook, no scheduled lessons, and no standardized grading. The piece deliberately distinguishes genuine unschooling from the common, looser home-educator claim that 'baking is learning,' arguing that an activity only counts as good education when it demonstrably develops a skill or piece of knowledge the child didn't already have, not merely when it happens to touch a curriculum-adjacent concept like measurement. The author lays out a five-step practical method -- observe the child's actual developmental and confidence level, encourage the interests that observation surfaces, notice specific progress rather than relying on worksheet-style 'evidencing,' contextualize learning by connecting a passion (like Minecraft) to broader real-world capability, and take learning forward by deliberately modeling adult problem-solving through 'active strewing' -- and grounds each step in a concrete example from her son's actual development, including his shift from memorizing Minecraft trivia to independently explaining how a solenoid works. The piece closes by insisting unschooling is not educational neglect but is in fact more time- and energy-intensive than conventional schooling-at-home, since it depends entirely on an actively engaged parent who knows the child well enough to supply the right next opportunity.
points: The 'baking is learning' critique sharpens what counts as genuine unschooling versus a comforting rationalization: an activity is educational when it demonstrably builds a skill or piece of knowledge the child didn't already have, not merely because it happens to touch a curriculum-adjacent concept.

The five-step method (observe, encourage interests, notice progress, contextualize, take learning forward) converts an abstract 'child-led' philosophy into an actionable parental practice, each step illustrated with a specific, falsifiable example from the author's own son's development.

The pinball-repair episode functions as proof-of-concept for 'active strewing': deliberately letting a child watch an adult solve a real problem by trial and error, without there being a course or curriculum for the skill at all, since none exists for pinball repair.

The essay explicitly rebuts the 'unschooling is educational neglect' charge by inverting the usual assumption: unschooling done well requires more parental time, attention, and engagement than a scheduled homeschool curriculum, not less, because there is no external structure doing any of the work.
quotes: Is that a solenoid?" he asked. I nodded. "Do you know how it works?" "Yes," said Bigger Boy, launching into a ten-minute explanation about how electricity creates a magnetic field that moves a physical rod.

I, personally, didn't take a course in pinball repair — there aren't any. I learned to repair a pinball machine the same way as most people in the hobby community: I bought a machine with multiple electrical faults and asked hobbyists online for help.
The reality is, although baking might be learning for kids who like baking, it's not automatically good home education.

I'd offer a (somewhat technical) definition of unschooling: Unschooling is a pedagogy where educators educate children by actively supporting them in developing their interests and passions, often by proactively facilitating new experiences and opportunities, and by assisting them in building their skills and knowledge to take advantage of these opportunities.

At school, the teacher tells you something you already know. Then, she tells you it again another four or five times, I don't know why. And, then, you handwritten evidence it. I don't enjoy evidencing.

Key to success is being an active, involved parent who knows their child(ren) well and has lots of time available to answer their questions, support their interests, and give them opportunities for personal growth.
